title: The highest-fiber legumes: a practical nutrition ranking

seo.title: Highest-fiber legumes: beans, lentils and chickpeas ranked
seo.meta_description: Beans, lentils and chickpeas are all rich in fiber when cooked. Compare fiber per 100 g and per realistic serving to see which differences matter.
seo.search_intent: Compare the fiber content of common cooked legumes and understand how much a normal serving contributes.

excerpt: Most cooked beans provide roughly 7–9 g of fiber per 100 g, while lentils and chickpeas are commonly around 7–8 g. A 1-cup serving can easily deliver about 12–17 g of fiber, so eating legumes regularly matters more than chasing a tiny difference between varieties.
content_html:
Legume rankings become misleading fast when dry beans are compared with cooked lentils. Cooking adds a large amount of water, so nutrients become less concentrated per 100 g even though they have not simply vanished.

For a useful plate-level comparison, the fairest starting point is cooked, drained legumes.

Fiber in common cooked legumes

The figures below are approximate and can shift with variety and cooking method.

Cooked legumeFiber/100 gFiber in about 1 cup
Navy beans~10 g~19 g
Pinto beans~9 g~15 g
Black beans~8.7 g~15 g
Lentils~7.9 g~16 g
Chickpeas~7.6 g~12–13 g
Split peas~8.3 g~16 g

The useful takeaway is not that one bean wins by a gram or two. It is that a normal bowl of legumes can supply a very large share of a day's fiber.

Why dry-legume numbers look so much higher

Dry lentils and beans contain little water. After cooking, they absorb water and weigh much more. Fiber and protein are therefore spread across a larger cooked weight, which lowers the value per 100 g without implying a comparable nutrient loss.

Does first place matter?

If one cup of beans provides roughly 15–19 g of fiber and chickpeas provide around 12–13 g, there is a difference, but it is much smaller than the difference between eating legumes and skipping them entirely.

U.S. guidance generally places adult fiber targets in the neighborhood of 25–38 g per day depending on age and sex. A generous serving of legumes can cover a substantial part of that.

Fiber comes with protein too

Legumes are not isolated fiber supplements. One cup of cooked lentils provides roughly 18 g of protein along with folate, iron and complex carbohydrates. Chickpeas provide a similar amount of protein in a cup, plus fiber and minerals.

That combination of fiber, protein, water and starch helps explain why legumes tend to be filling.

Canned beans still count

Canned legumes remain a useful source of fiber. Rinsing them can lower some of the sodium in the packing liquid without washing away the structural fiber inside the bean.

The practical answer

If maximum concentration is your only criterion, several beans sit near the top. In everyday eating, however, beans, lentils and chickpeas are close enough that serving size, frequency and variety matter more than a narrow ranking.

faq.question: Which legumes have the most fiber?
faq.answer: Several cooked beans provide around 8–10 g of fiber per 100 g, with lentils and chickpeas close behind at roughly 7–8 g.

faq.question: How much fiber is in a cup of legumes?
faq.answer: Depending on the legume, a cup commonly provides about 12–19 g of fiber.

faq.question: Do canned beans still have fiber?
faq.answer: Yes. Canned beans remain fiber-rich, and rinsing them mainly helps reduce sodium rather than fiber.
